passages.title: The Middle Octave
passages.text:
My grandfather tuned pianos for forty years, and for most of those years he refused to own one. "A tuner with a piano at home," he told me once, "is like a baker who eats his own bread. He stops tasting it." So the upright that arrived at his house the spring I turned twelve was a surprise to everyone, including, I think, him.

It had belonged to Mrs. Okafor, whose church had replaced it with an electric keyboard. The movers set it against the dining-room wall, and for a week my grandfather walked past it as though it were a stranger who had come to stay without being invited. He did not lift the lid. He did not, as far as I could tell, even look at it.

On Saturday he called me in from the yard. He had laid his tools out on a dish towel—the tuning hammer, the rubber mutes, the felt strip—in the same order he used in other people's houses. "You'll do the middle octave," he said. I said I didn't know how. "Nobody knows how," he said. "They learn to hear it."

What he meant, I found out, was that a string slightly out of tune with its neighbor doesn't sound wrong so much as restless. Two notes that should agree produce a slow wavering, a beat, like someone breathing just out of step with you. My job was to turn the pin until the breathing stopped. For the first hour I heard nothing at all. Then, near noon, I heard it everywhere: in the piano, in the refrigerator's hum against the clock radio, in the two of us humming the same note while we waited for each other.

My grandfather did not praise me. When I finished the octave he played a single chord, listened, and moved one pin a hair's width with his own hand. Then he put the hammer back on the towel—at my place, not his—and went to make lunch.

I understood years later that he had not needed a piano. He had needed someone to hand his ear to, and an instrument was simply the only way he knew to do it. That afternoon, though, I knew only that the house sounded different, and that when I walked past the dining-room wall, I no longer felt I was passing a stranger.

passages.title: NATURAL SCIENCE: "The Night Shift" (an original essay written for this practice set)
passages.text:
On a summer afternoon in the desert, a plant faces a dilemma that most of us never consider. To grow, it needs carbon dioxide from the air, which enters through tiny pores in its leaves or stems called stomata. But every open pore is also an exit. Water vapor escapes through the same openings, and in hot, dry air it escapes quickly. A plant that keeps its pores open all day may run short of water; a plant that keeps them shut may run short of carbon.

Many desert plants, including most cacti, have settled this dilemma by changing their schedule. Rather than opening their stomata in daylight, as most plants do, they open them at night, when the air is cooler and more humid and far less water is lost. The carbon dioxide they take in is not used right away. Instead, the plant stores it, chemically bound in an acid, inside its cells.

When the sun rises, the stomata close, sealing the plant against the heat. Only then does the stored carbon go to work. Sunlight powers photosynthesis, and the plant releases carbon from its acid store and builds it into sugars, all without opening a single pore. In effect, the plant has separated two tasks that most plants perform together: gathering carbon at night and using it by day.

Botanists call this strategy crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, after the stonecrop family of succulents in which it was first studied. The name is clumsy, but the idea is elegant. A plant using CAM can capture carbon while losing only a small fraction of the water that a typical plant would lose.

The strategy has a cost. Storing carbon overnight takes energy, and the amount a plant can store is limited by the size of its cells. CAM plants therefore tend to grow slowly. Where water is plentiful in the soil, they are usually outgrown by faster-growing neighbors. The very adjustment that lets a cactus thrive in the desert would be a handicap in a well-watered meadow.

Perhaps that is the most useful lesson the cactus offers: an adaptation is not simply an improvement. It is a trade, and whether the trade pays depends on where the organism lives. A strategy that looks like brilliance in one place can look like weakness in another.

candidates.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: a grandfather's lifelong refusal to own the instrument he worked on.
choices.B: a grandfather using an unexpected piano to pass his skill to the narrator.
choices.C: the narrator's struggle to win a grandfather's praise and approval.
choices.D: the history of a piano that a church gave away to a neighbor.

candidates.evidence: He had needed someone to hand his ear to
candidates.explanation: Most of the passage follows the tuning lesson, and the last paragraph names its point: the grandfather needed "someone to hand his ear to," and the piano was the means.

A.rationale: The refusal is only the opening setup in paragraph 1; the passage is about what happens once the piano arrives.

C.rationale: The grandfather "did not praise" the narrator, but the narrator is never shown struggling for praise.

D.rationale: The piano's origin gets one sentence; it is background, not the focus.

hints: Which paragraphs take up most of the passage?
What does the last paragraph say the episode was really about?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the passage in one sentence before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: A main-idea answer must cover the whole passage, not its opening.

candidates.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred that the grandfather put the hammer back "at my place, not his" (paragraph 5) in order to:

choices.A: indicate that the narrator was expected to put away the tools.
choices.B: show that he no longer intended to tune pianos for others.
choices.C: quietly acknowledge the narrator as a fellow tuner.
choices.D: remind the narrator that one pin still needed adjusting.

candidates.explanation: The grandfather gives no spoken praise, but placing the hammer at the narrator's place treats the narrator as the one who now holds the tool; paragraph 6 confirms he was handing on his ear.

A.rationale: Nothing suggests a cleanup task; he leaves to make lunch, and the gesture concerns whose place the hammer belongs to.

B.rationale: The passage never suggests he is quitting his work.

D.rationale: He has already adjusted the pin himself before setting the hammer down.

hints: Whose place did the hammer belong at before?
How does paragraph 6 explain what the grandfather wanted?

strategy.explanation: Connect the gesture to the explanation in the final paragraph.

candidates.remember: Unspoken gestures in fiction often carry the key meaning.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "agree" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: Two notes that should agree produce a slow wavering
candidates.explanation: The sentence concerns two notes whose sounds should line up; when they don't, they produce a beat. "Agree" here means match in pitch.

A.rationale: Notes cannot consent; this is a common meaning that does not fit sounds.

B.rationale: Notes have no opinions; this is the everyday meaning of "agree."

C.rationale: Promising does not apply to sounds.

hints: What are the two things that should agree?
Substitute each choice into the sentence.

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own phrase, then match.

candidates.remember: Test each meaning in the sentence itself.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the grandfather explained his refusal to own a piano by claiming that a tuner who owns one:

choices.A: loses the sensitivity to sound that the work requires.
choices.B: finds that a piano kept at home goes out of tune.
choices.C: cannot afford an instrument as well as the tools.
choices.D: is distracted from paid work by playing for pleasure.

candidates.evidence: is like a baker who eats his own bread. He stops tasting it.
candidates.explanation: The baker comparison means that constant exposure dulls the senses: a tuner with a piano at home would stop really hearing it.

B.rationale: Tuning stability is never mentioned as his reason.

D.rationale: He says nothing about playing for pleasure or distraction.

hints: Reread the baker comparison.
What does "stops tasting it" mean for a tuner?

strategy.explanation: Find the quoted explanation and translate the comparison.

candidates.remember: Translate a comparison back into the literal claim.

candidates.stem: The comparison of the piano to "a stranger who had come to stay without being invited" (paragraph 2) primarily serves to:

choices.A: convey the grandfather's uneasy reluctance to engage with the piano.
choices.B: suggest that the piano had been damaged during the move.
choices.C: indicate that Mrs. Okafor had not wanted to give the piano away.
choices.D: foreshadow that the piano would later be returned to the church.

candidates.evidence: He did not lift the lid. He did not, as far as I could tell, even look at it.
candidates.explanation: The simile is followed by details of avoidance (he did not lift the lid or look at it), so it conveys his discomfort with the unwanted presence of the piano.

B.rationale: Nothing in the passage mentions damage.

C.rationale: The "uninvited" feeling is the grandfather's, not Mrs. Okafor's; her wishes are never described.

D.rationale: The piano stays; by the end the narrator no longer feels it is a stranger.

hints: Whose feelings does the comparison describe?
What do the sentences right after it show?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentences around the comparison to see what it describes.

candidates.remember: Figurative language usually reveals a character's attitude.

candidates.stem: The final sentence of the passage most directly echoes which earlier detail?

choices.A: The grandfather's comparison of a tuner to a baker
choices.B: The tools laid out on a towel in a fixed order
choices.C: The grandfather walking past the piano as if it were a guest he had not invited
choices.D: The slow wavering produced by two notes out of tune

candidates.evidence: I no longer felt I was passing a stranger
candidates.explanation: The last sentence returns to walking past the dining-room wall and to the word "stranger," the image from paragraph 2 of the piano as an uninvited stranger; the echo marks how the piano has changed from intruder to part of the household.

A.rationale: The baker comparison is about dulled senses, not about passing something by.

B.rationale: The towel and tools do not reappear in the final sentence.

D.rationale: The final sentence mentions the house sounding different, but its closing image is passing a stranger, not the beat.

hints: Which words in the last sentence appeared earlier?
Where did the image of a "stranger" first appear?

strategy.explanation: Match repeated words and images across paragraphs.

candidates.remember: Endings often call back to an image from the opening.

candidates.stem: Compared with what the narrator knew at age twelve, the adult narrator in paragraph 6 recognizes:

choices.A: that the piano had been badly out of tune when it first arrived.
choices.B: the grandfather's real purpose in bringing the narrator into the tuning.
choices.C: that the grandfather had secretly wanted a piano of his own all along.
choices.D: that the narrator's tuning of the middle octave had been slightly flawed.

candidates.evidence: I understood years later that he had not needed a piano. He had needed someone to hand his ear to
candidates.explanation: The adult realization is about the grandfather's motive: he wanted to pass on his ear, and the piano was only the means. At twelve the narrator knew only that the house sounded different.

A.rationale: Whether the piano was out of tune on arrival is never addressed as a later realization.

C.rationale: Paragraph 6 says the opposite: he "had not needed a piano."

D.rationale: The narrator saw him move one pin at the time; that is not something learned "years later."

hints: What does "years later" introduce?
What did the narrator know "that afternoon"?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices the passage contradicts or that the narrator knew at the time.

candidates.remember: Separate what a narrator knew then from what they understand now.

candidates.stem: The narrator's statement that near noon "I heard it everywhere" (paragraph 4) most nearly suggests that the narrator:

choices.A: was growing tired and easily distracted by noise.
choices.B: found the house unusually noisy that day.
choices.C: noticed that the refrigerator and radio needed repair.
choices.D: had learned to perceive a sound that had been there all along.

candidates.evidence: For the first hour I heard nothing at all. Then, near noon, I heard it everywhere
candidates.explanation: After an hour of hearing nothing, the narrator suddenly hears the beat in many ordinary sounds: the skill of hearing it has been learned, as the grandfather said it would be.

A.rationale: Hearing the beat is presented as success, not distraction.

B.rationale: The sounds are ordinary household sounds; what changed was the narrator's hearing.

C.rationale: The beat between two hums is not a sign of broken appliances.

hints: What could the narrator hear in the first hour?
What changed by noon: the house or the listener?

strategy.explanation: Predict "the narrator learned to hear it," then match.

candidates.remember: Look for what changes in the character, not the setting.

candidates.stem: The grandfather's remark "Nobody knows how. They learn to hear it" (paragraph 3) best reflects his view that tuning skill:

choices.A: is a natural gift that cannot really be taught.
choices.B: depends mainly on owning the proper tools.
choices.C: develops through practiced listening, not prior knowledge.
choices.D: must be learned from a teacher before any practice.

candidates.evidence: "Nobody knows how," he said. "They learn to hear it."
candidates.explanation: "Nobody knows how" means no one starts with the skill; "they learn to hear it" means it is acquired by listening in practice, which is exactly what the narrator then does.

A.rationale: "Nobody knows how" can sound like the skill is unreachable, but "they learn" says it is acquired.

B.rationale: The tools are set out, but the remark is about hearing, not equipment.

D.rationale: He gives the narrator the task with no prior lesson; learning happens while doing it.

hints: Read both halves of the remark together.
How does the narrator actually learn?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that fit only half of the remark.

candidates.remember: Read the whole quotation; half of it can mislead.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the word "settled" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: Many desert plants, including most cacti, have settled this dilemma by changing their schedule.
candidates.explanation: The plants have "settled this dilemma," the problem from paragraph 1, by changing when they open their pores. In this context "settled" means resolved.

A.rationale: "Settled" can mean 'came to live in a place,' and the sentence mentions desert plants, but here the object is a dilemma, not a region.

B.rationale: "Calmed" fits settling a person or a stomach, not a dilemma.

C.rationale: "Paid off" fits settling a debt, not a dilemma.

hints: What is being settled?
What does one do to a dilemma?

strategy.explanation: Predict 'solved,' then choose the closest meaning.

candidates.remember: Check the word's object before choosing a meaning.

candidates.stem: Which choice correctly describes the sequence of events in a CAM plant, as presented in the passage?

choices.A: By day, stomata open to take in carbon; at night, carbon is stored as an acid.
choices.B: At night, stomata open and carbon is stored as an acid; by day, stomata close and the carbon is used.
choices.C: At night, stomata close and carbon is used to make sugar; by day, carbon is stored.
choices.D: By day, stomata close and carbon is stored; at night, sunlight releases it for sugar.

candidates.evidence: gathering carbon at night and using it by day
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2: stomata open at night and carbon is stored in an acid. Paragraph 3: stomata close at sunrise, and the stored carbon is released and built into sugars using sunlight.

A.rationale: This reverses the timing: CAM plants open their stomata at night, not by day.

C.rationale: This reverses both steps; sugar-making needs sunlight and happens by day.

D.rationale: Sunlight is not available at night, and carbon is stored at night, not by day.

hints: When are the stomata open?
When is sunlight available to make sugar?

strategy.explanation: Check each half of every choice against paragraphs 2 and 3.

candidates.remember: In sequence questions, check both halves of each choice.

candidates.stem: Which situation would best illustrate the claim in the final paragraph?

choices.A: A crop variety that produces more grain whenever farmers add fertilizer.
choices.B: A desert plant that saves water by opening its pores at night.
choices.C: A bird species that thrives in many very different climates.
choices.D: Thick fur that keeps an animal warm in the Arctic but overheats it in the tropics.

candidates.evidence: whether the trade pays depends on where the organism lives
candidates.explanation: The final paragraph claims an adaptation is a trade whose value depends on where the organism lives. Thick fur that helps in the Arctic but hurts in the tropics shows the same trait being an advantage in one place and a weakness in another.

A.rationale: This is a simple improvement with no trade-off and no dependence on place.

B.rationale: This shows only the benefit, in one place; the claim is about value changing with location.

C.rationale: A species that succeeds everywhere shows no dependence on place.

hints: State the final paragraph's claim in your own words.
Which choice shows one trait helping in one place and hurting in another?

strategy.explanation: Test each choice for both parts: a trade-off and dependence on location.

candidates.remember: Application questions: match the claim's structure, not its topic.
